scenario: We are integrating upstream Jolt Physics directly into a custom C++ engine for a 120 Hz multiplayer prototype. The current plan is: call JPH::RegisterDefaultAllocator and Factory::sInstance = new Factory; let Jolt create whatever worker threads it needs; use one broad object layer and make every pair collide; create Body objects during gameplay and keep their BodyID values forever; serialize raw BodyID and transforms for rollback; call PhysicsSystem::Update(deltaTime, 1, tempAllocator, jobSystem) from a variable render loop; use CharacterVirtual for players, VehicleConstraint for cars, and SoftBodyCreationSettings for cloth; assume deterministic replay across Windows/Linux if every client uses the same seed; ship after HelloWorld passes. Give an implementation review and a corrected integration/validation plan.

baseline.response:
The current plan is suitable as a small API experiment, but it is not safe as an engine integration or a multiplayer shipping plan. It leaves ownership, threading, collision filtering, fixed-step timing, object identity, rollback state, and subsystem validation undefined. “HelloWorld passes” proves only that one build can initialize and step a trivial world.

## Problems in the current plan

1. **Initialization is incomplete and has no shutdown contract.** Registering the allocator and assigning `Factory::sInstance` is only part of process initialization. Pin one Jolt revision and verify the exact initialization sequence for that revision, including trace/assert hooks and type registration. Define the reverse teardown order as well: stop physics work, join the engine-owned workers, destroy worlds and all objects that depend on registered types, unregister types, then delete and clear the factory. Reinitializing or unloading while Jolt objects remain alive should be forbidden.

2. **The engine must own the job system.** Jolt should not be expected to invent an appropriate worker topology. Create a long-lived job system explicitly, choose its worker count from the engine’s thread budget, and keep it alive for every update that can reference it. Decide whether Jolt gets a dedicated pool or an adapter to the engine scheduler. In either case, document shutdown, worker affinity, maximum jobs/barriers, oversubscription with rendering and networking, and what happens when a physics job fails. Create a bounded temporary allocator from measured scene demand rather than an arbitrary sample value.

3. **One object layer with every pair colliding is not an acceptable filter design.** It will waste broad-phase and narrow-phase work and makes triggers, static scenery, characters, vehicles, projectiles, and query-only objects difficult to reason about. Start with a small explicit collision matrix derived from gameplay rules. Map object layers to a smaller set of broad-phase layers, and implement both object-vs-broad-phase and object-pair filters. Test the matrix in both directions. Keep query masks and sensor behavior explicit instead of relying on accidental pair-filter behavior.

4. **`BodyID` is a transient physics handle, not a permanent network identity.** A body can be removed and destroyed, and an ID slot may later be reused with a different sequence value. Keeping IDs forever or sending raw IDs across machines couples game state to one process’s allocation history. Give each replicated object a stable engine/network ID plus a generation. Maintain a validated mapping from that identity to the current `BodyID`, invalidate it during remove/destroy, and reject stale generations. Route body access through a narrow physics-world API so gameplay cannot retain unchecked handles or access bodies concurrently without the required locking discipline.

5. **Creating bodies during play needs an explicit lifecycle.** Separate create, add/activate, deactivate, remove, and destroy operations. Queue lifecycle commands at defined tick boundaries; do not mutate the world unpredictably from render, network, or worker callbacks. Record spawn/despawn events in rollback history. Establish ownership for shapes, constraints, user data, listeners, and engine components, and test shutdown and rapid create/destroy churn.

6. **A variable render-loop update breaks the stated 120 Hz simulation contract.** Accumulate real time outside physics and consume fixed `1 / 120` second ticks. Pass that fixed value to the pinned revision’s `PhysicsSystem::Update` signature, with collision/integration step choices justified by tests. Never stretch the physics delta to catch up. Cap work per rendered frame, expose an overload metric, and choose an explicit overload policy such as slowing presentation, dropping a client from prediction, or resynchronizing. Publish completed physics snapshots and interpolate presentation between them; the renderer must not own simulation transforms.

7. **Transforms plus a random seed do not constitute rollback state.** Rollback must account for at least creation/destruction, pose, linear and angular velocity, activation/sleep state, relevant motion properties, constraints, character state, vehicle inputs/state, and any gameplay state that affects forces or contacts. Internal caches and floating-point execution can diverge even when seeds match. Do not claim deterministic replay across Windows and Linux without evidence from the exact compiler, flags, CPU policy, Jolt revision, and content. Prefer an authoritative server with reconciliation. If client rollback is required, use stable game IDs, deterministic command ordering, tick-stamped inputs, periodic authoritative snapshots, state hashes for diagnosis, and a recovery path when replay diverges.

8. **The three high-level features are separate integrations, not proof that the base world works.** `CharacterVirtual` is not simply a normal rigid body: define its per-tick update order, collision/query filters, supporting-body behavior, contact callbacks, slope and step policy, and the state replicated for correction. `VehicleConstraint` needs a chassis lifecycle, wheel collision strategy, constraint registration/removal, input ordering, and validation under suspension/contact edge cases. Cloth through `SoftBodyCreationSettings` needs asset conversion, material/constraint policy, collision layers, memory and CPU budgets, sleeping/visibility policy, and a networking decision; replicating every soft-body particle is unlikely to fit a prototype budget.

## Corrected integration plan

### 1. Freeze the integration boundary

Pin the Jolt commit or release, build options, compiler, floating-point settings, target architectures, and debug/profile/release configurations. Wrap Jolt behind engine-owned world, body, query, character, vehicle, and soft-body interfaces. Keep Jolt headers and handles out of network packets and long-lived gameplay save data. Record the exact configuration in captures and crash reports.

### 2. Build a process/world lifecycle harness

Implement process initialization and teardown with explicit allocator, diagnostics, factory/type registration, temporary allocator, and job-system ownership. Add a minimal world configuration with declared capacities and filters. Exercise initialize-create-step-destroy-shutdown repeatedly in one process, including an empty world and a world destroyed while many objects have recently been removed. Run this under the platform memory/thread diagnostic tools available to the project.

### 3. Define collision and query policy

Write the gameplay collision matrix first. Assign object and broad-phase layers, then implement and unit-test every allowed and denied pair. Add tests for ray/shape queries, sensors, static-vs-static rejection, character queries, vehicle wheels, and soft-body interaction. Profile candidate layer layouts with representative counts rather than accepting the broadest layout for convenience.

### 4. Define identity, commands, and ownership

Use stable engine IDs with generations and a per-world mapping to transient body handles. Queue body creation, activation, mutation, removal, and destruction as tick-addressed commands. Make one subsystem responsible for applying those commands and publishing results. Validate stale handles, duplicate destroys, world teardown, and allocation-slot reuse. Store engine identity in user data only as a lookup aid, not as a substitute for validating ownership.

### 5. Implement the fixed-step scheduler

Run exactly 120 simulation ticks per simulated second using a fixed accumulator. Establish a deterministic order for network input ingestion, queued lifecycle changes, controller/vehicle input, force application, physics update, event extraction, snapshot publication, and render interpolation. Measure tick time, temporary allocator high-water mark, active body count, contact count, jobs, and backlog. Define a maximum catch-up budget and test long frames, pauses, and clock correction.

### 6. Integrate features incrementally

First validate rigid bodies, constraints, queries, contact delivery, and activation. Then add one `CharacterVirtual` path with controlled slopes, steps, moving platforms, penetration recovery, and server correction. Add vehicles only after chassis/constraint lifecycle is stable. Add soft bodies last, with a declared local-only, server-authored, or replicated role and a hard performance budget. Each feature gets its own collision/filter and create/destroy tests.

### 7. Choose and prove the multiplayer model

Start with server authority and tick-stamped inputs. Decide separately which objects are predicted, interpolated, or server-only. For any rollback scope, define a versioned snapshot schema in engine terms, stable entity mapping, retained tick window, spawn/despawn log, replay input log, hash diagnostics, and authoritative correction. Run replay tests first on the same binary, then across supported Windows/Linux builds. Treat every mismatch as data to diagnose; never convert “same seed” into a determinism guarantee.

### 8. Replace HelloWorld with release gates

Keep HelloWorld as a bootstrap smoke test, then require automated tests for initialization failure and teardown, layer/filter truth tables, body-handle reuse, command ordering, concurrent queries, contact listener lifetime, fixed-step behavior under variable rendering, character correction, vehicle and cloth lifecycle, and rollback divergence recovery. Add long-running soak tests with creation/destruction churn and representative peak loads. Run debug/profile/release builds on every supported platform, capture CPU and memory distributions rather than one average, and test network latency, jitter, loss, reordering, late input, and resynchronization.

Before shipping, require measured budgets for worst-case physics tick time at 120 Hz, memory and temporary allocation, worker utilization, active bodies/constraints/contacts, snapshot bandwidth and retained rollback memory. Require no stale-handle or shutdown failures in stress runs, no unexplained state-hash divergence in the supported replay scope, and a demonstrated recovery path for overload and network desynchronization.

The immediate milestone should therefore be a fixed-step, engine-owned Jolt world with explicit jobs, filters, identity/lifetime rules, and rigid-body rollback diagnostics. Character, vehicle, and cloth work should not begin in parallel until that foundation passes lifecycle, timing, and authority tests.

attempts.response:
## Review verdict

The current plan is suitable only as a first smoke-test sketch. It is not safe for a 120 Hz multiplayer integration, because ownership, stepping, identity, rollback, determinism, error handling, and module maturity are all underspecified or incorrect.

Use Jolt v5.6.0 commit `e77f175595e64cb44218cc9d9d56fc365ad0e36a` as the source snapshot for this plan, but first verify that it is the version actually being built. Freeze and record the tag/commit, compiler and standard library, platform and architecture, float/double mode, SIMD and floating-point policy, Jolt and host defines, build role, allocator/job model, enabled modules, content revision, and capture provenance. Do not infer the running binary from `master` or from this snapshot.

## Problems in the proposed integration

1. **Initialization is incomplete.** `RegisterDefaultAllocator` must precede every Jolt allocation or API call, but the process also needs host trace/assert hooks, `Factory::sInstance`, `RegisterTypes`, retained allocators/jobs/filters/listeners, `PhysicsSystem::Init`, and an explicit reverse-order shutdown. Merely allocating the factory is not enough.

2. **Jolt does not own the engine's thread budget.** The host must construct, size, retain, and shut down the `JobSystem`. The integration must define callback threads, worker barriers, job failure behavior, temporary-allocator exhaustion, and how workers are joined before world dependencies disappear.

3. **One collide-everything layer conflates separate policies.** `ObjectLayer` controls gameplay pair policy, `BroadPhaseLayer` partitions broad-phase storage, `ObjectVsBroadPhaseLayerFilter` prunes object-versus-partition work, and `ObjectLayerPairFilter` decides object-pair collisions. Define each deliberately, make the pair matrix symmetric, and test both argument orders plus sensor and query masks.

4. **`BodyID` is not permanent identity.** It is local to one `PhysicsSystem`, contains reuse protection, can become stale, and may eventually be reused. The correct body lifecycle is create, add, remove, then destroy. Give every replicated object a stable host ID plus generation, map that identity to the current `BodyID`, and invalidate the mapping on removal or destruction. Check body-lock success before dereferencing; use `BodyLockMultiRead`/`BodyLockMultiWrite` for groups. Permit no-lock access only behind a documented callback or lock guarantee.

5. **Raw IDs and transforms do not constitute rollback state.** `StateRecorder` covers Jolt simulation state, but it does not recreate host structure, gameplay variables, or add/remove history. Restore also depends on compatible settings and matching IDs and call order. A rollback frame must retain the Jolt state stream together with stable identity mappings, ordered spawn/despawn events, ordered inputs, controller/vehicle/gameplay state outside the recorder, content/config version, and recovery metadata.

6. **A variable render-loop step breaks the 120 Hz contract.** One host scheduler must accumulate elapsed real time and consume fixed `1 / 120` simulation ticks. Each tick makes exactly one v5.6 call of the form `PhysicsSystem::Update(fixedDelta, collisionSteps, tempAllocator, jobSystem)`. `collisionSteps` must be measured for the content rather than copied from a sample. Rendering uses interpolation between committed simulation states. Bound catch-up work and define overload recovery without stretching the fixed delta.

7. **Update errors cannot be ignored.** Inspect all returned `EPhysicsUpdateError` flags every tick. Capacity, allocator, contact, or body-pair failures need an explicit policy such as stop, controlled degradation, resize at a safe boundary, or authoritative resync. HelloWorld capacities and its 10 MiB temporary allocator are examples, not production defaults.

8. **A shared seed does not prove cross-platform determinism.** Enable `JPH_CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC` as a prerequisite, then also hold source, defines, precision, SIMD/FP policy, content, inputs, thread-visible command order, and build role constant. Normalize unordered broad-phase queries, collectors, callbacks/contacts, and active-body results by stable host identity before they affect gameplay or hashes. Windows/Linux equality must be demonstrated with per-tick evidence.

9. **The selected modules need separate ownership and maturity gates.** `CharacterVirtual` is host-owned and explicitly updated at the fixed tick; its v5.6 contact API, filters, supporting-body behavior, callback threading, input, and external state must be version-gated and included in rollback. A vehicle needs a retained chassis, `VehicleCollisionTester`, and `VehicleConstraint`; add the constraint, apply input in a fixed tick order, and remove it before destroying retained vehicle objects. `SoftBodyCreationSettings` uses the normal add/remove/destroy lifetime, but soft bodies and GPU hair are WIP in this snapshot. Cloth needs an explicit local-only, authoritative, or replicated scope and production evidence before shipment.

10. **HelloWorld is only the first rung.** Passing it validates a narrow initialization/update/shutdown path, not rollback correctness, module behavior, target performance, or cross-platform replay.

## Corrected integration plan

### 1. Freeze the build contract

Create a machine-readable build fingerprint containing the exact Jolt revision and every compiler, precision, SIMD/FP, define, platform, job-model, module, content, and build-role choice. Verify compatible definitions across all translation units. Treat binary state streams as pinned-version artifacts, not durable cross-version save files.

### 2. Make process and world ownership explicit

Initialize in dependency order:

1. Register the default allocator before any other Jolt call; install host trace and assert hooks.
2. Allocate `Factory::sInstance` and call `RegisterTypes`.
3. Create and retain the temporary allocator, host-sized `JobSystem`, broad-phase mapping, both filters, and listeners.
4. Construct the world and call `PhysicsSystem::Init` with measured capacities and those retained filter objects.
5. Register listeners, then create and add bodies and constraints.

Shutdown must first stop fixed-tick submission and callbacks, join workers, remove and destroy constraints and bodies, unregister listeners, destroy worlds and retained dependencies, call `UnregisterTypes`, then delete and clear `Factory::sInstance`. Exercise repeated initialize/world-create/world-destroy/shutdown cycles.

### 3. Define collision and query policy

Start from gameplay categories such as static world, dynamic body, player/controller support, vehicle, sensor, and soft body. Specify a symmetric object-layer pair matrix. Map object layers to broad-phase layers independently, then implement object-versus-broad-phase pruning. Unit-test the full matrix in both orders and test ray/shape/overlap queries and sensors separately. Consume collection results as sets or stable-sort them by host identity.

### 4. Put structural mutation behind tick boundaries

Queue spawn, add, remove, constraint, and destroy commands and commit them at an owned fixed-tick phase in a deterministic total order. Maintain a host identity/generation to current-Jolt-handle table. Never serialize a raw `BodyID` or retained constraint pointer as a network identity. Centralize lock-checked body access in the engine wrapper and make any no-lock precondition explicit.

### 5. Install one fixed-step scheduler

The simulation owner accumulates real time, consumes zero or more fixed `1 / 120` ticks up to a declared catch-up cap, and leaves a fractional remainder for render interpolation. For every tick:

1. Order and apply tick-stamped structural commands and inputs.
2. Update host-owned characters and vehicle controls in a documented order.
3. Call the pinned v5.6 `PhysicsSystem::Update` once with the fixed delta and measured `collisionSteps`.
4. Inspect and record `EPhysicsUpdateError` flags.
5. Normalize externally consumed unordered results, capture the rollback frame, and compute a diagnostic state hash.

Define what happens when the accumulator exceeds the cap; do not compensate by changing the simulation delta.

### 6. Design rollback around structure plus state

At each rollback boundary, capture the Jolt `StateRecorder` stream plus ordered inputs, structural events, stable-ID mappings and generations, external character/vehicle/gameplay state, content/config fingerprint, update errors, and recovery metadata. To restore, reconstruct the matching world structure and IDs in the recorded call order, restore the compatible Jolt state, restore host state, then replay tick-stamped commands through the same fixed-tick path. Compare per-tick hashes and trigger authoritative correction/resync if restore or replay diverges.

### 7. Prove determinism instead of assuming it

First prove replay repeatability with the same binary. Then run an evidence matrix for every supported Windows/Linux compiler, architecture, and build role using identical tick-stamped commands and a stable host command order. Record per-tick hashes and the first divergent tick. Preserve the inputs, structural events, job configuration, update-error flags, normalized result sets, and build fingerprint needed to bisect a mismatch. The determinism define and seed are necessary inputs, not acceptance criteria.

### 8. Gate optional modules independently

Give `CharacterVirtual`, vehicles, and cloth separate owners, rollback contracts, fixed-tick ordering, callback rules, capacity/performance budgets, and version-specific tests. Route generic controller movement, vehicle dynamics, cloth design, networking/authority, regression testing, and profiling decisions to their respective subsystem work; keep this integration focused on the Jolt-specific seams. Do not put WIP soft-body behavior on the critical replicated path without measured evidence and a recovery strategy.

## Validation and release gates

Run the following ladder against the frozen configuration:

1. Build and run pinned v5.6.0 HelloWorld as an initialization/update/shutdown smoke test.
2. Build and run upstream UnitTests for every selected compiler, define set, precision mode, and build role.
3. Run official Samples covering every API actually used: layers/queries, bodies, constraints, `CharacterVirtual`, vehicles, and soft bodies where applicable.
4. Run pinned determinism and `StateRecorder` save/restore tests, including mismatched structure, stale IDs, capacity errors, and allocator/job fault injection.
5. Run host tests for the 120 Hz accumulator, catch-up limits, spawn/despawn ordering, rollback and replay, per-tick hash divergence, callback threading, repeated shutdown, and authority/resync under jitter, loss, and reordering.
6. Run PerformanceTest and host profiling on target hardware and real content. Report p50/p95/p99 physics tick time and high-water budgets for temporary memory, jobs/barriers, bodies, pairs, constraints, contacts, rollback memory, and bandwidth.

Promotion requires every used module and every supported platform/build role to pass its applicable rung with no unhandled update errors. HelloWorld passing is the start of validation, not a ship criterion.

attempts.response:
The proposed integration is not production-safe. It has lifecycle gaps, gives thread and identity ownership to the wrong layer, uses a variable simulation step, and treats smoke-test success and a shared seed as stronger evidence than they are.

Use the following as the integration baseline. The API details below are pinned to Jolt v5.6.0, commit `e77f175595e64cb44218cc9d9d56fc365ad0e36a`; first verify that this is the source actually being built. Record the compiler/STL, platform and architecture, float/double precision, SIMD and floating-point policy, every Jolt and host define, build role, allocator/job configuration, enabled modules, and content revision. In particular, do not infer the binary's contract from `master` or from this pinned reference alone.

## Review of the current plan

- Initialization is incomplete. `RegisterDefaultAllocator` must precede every Jolt allocation or API call, but creating `Factory::sInstance` is not enough: install the host's trace/assert hooks, create the factory, and call `RegisterTypes`. The reverse sequence must be implemented at shutdown, including `UnregisterTypes` and deleting and clearing the factory.
- Jolt does not choose the engine's worker-thread budget. The host owns the long-lived temporary allocator and `JobSystem`, including their capacity, worker count, failure behavior, barriers, and shutdown. The host must also own the filters and listeners for at least as long as the `PhysicsSystem` uses them.
- One broad object layer with every pair enabled conflates three separate concerns: gameplay object-pair policy, broad-phase partitioning, and object-vs-broad-phase pruning. It is neither an explicit correctness policy nor a scalable default.
- `BodyID` is a world-local reusable handle, not a permanent gameplay, network, or save identity. Keeping it forever and serializing it raw will eventually permit stale-handle use or aliasing after reuse. Body ownership still follows create, add, remove, destroy.
- Saving a transform and raw `BodyID` is not rollback. `StateRecorder` covers Jolt simulation state but does not reconstruct the host's bodies, gameplay variables, or structural add/remove history; restore also expects compatible settings and matching IDs/call order.
- Calling `PhysicsSystem::Update` from a variable render loop makes the simulation depend on rendering cadence. At 120 Hz, a single host scheduler must feed fixed `1 / 120` ticks from an accumulator. `collisionSteps` is the v5.6 argument; choose it from measured stability/quality needs, not by copying an old substep recipe.
- A common seed is not a cross-platform determinism guarantee. `JPH_CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC` is only a prerequisite. Source, defines, precision, SIMD/FP behavior, inputs, and thread-visible call order must also match, and unordered results must be normalized before they influence gameplay or hashes.
- The selected feature modules have integration-specific obligations. `CharacterVirtual` is not an ordinary rigid body; `VehicleConstraint` is also a step listener; and soft bodies are WIP with behavior and API boundaries that differ from regular bodies and constraints.
- HelloWorld proves only that a minimal initialization/update/shutdown path works. It does not validate the used modules, rollback, determinism, capacity handling, concurrency, shutdown safety, performance, or production content.

## Corrected integration plan

### 1. Freeze and reproduce the build

Vendor or otherwise pin v5.6.0 at the exact commit above. Make the build manifest emit all compatibility inputs: compiler/STL, target architecture, precision mode, SIMD/FP policy, defines including the determinism define, build role, enabled modules, allocator/job model, and content/config revision. Add a runtime/build fingerprint to captures and rollback diagnostics. Reject peers or stored state whose compatibility fields do not match; do not treat Jolt binary state as a cross-version format.

### 2. Make process and world ownership explicit

Initialize in dependency order:

1. Call `RegisterDefaultAllocator` before any other Jolt use and install host-appropriate trace/assert handling.
2. Allocate `Factory::sInstance` and call `RegisterTypes`.
3. Construct host-owned, long-lived temporary allocation, `JobSystem`, broad-phase interface, `ObjectVsBroadPhaseLayerFilter`, `ObjectLayerPairFilter`, and listeners.
4. Construct the world and call `PhysicsSystem::Init` with measured capacities and those retained dependencies.
5. Register listeners, then create and add bodies and constraints.

Define which threads may invoke every callback, where structural commands are queued, and which tick boundary applies them. Own job submission and barriers in the engine. Treat temporary-memory exhaustion, job failure, and capacity exhaustion as explicit failure paths.

Shutdown in reverse dependency order: stop update submission, stop callbacks, join the host workers, remove step listeners and constraints, remove/destroy bodies, unregister listeners, destroy worlds and retained filters/allocators/job resources, call `UnregisterTypes`, then delete and clear `Factory::sInstance`. Exercise repeated init/world-destroy/shutdown rather than assuming process exit hides lifetime bugs.

### 3. Specify layers and filtering

Define object layers from gameplay semantics—for example static world, dynamic bodies, player proxies, vehicles, sensors, and any soft-body categories actually required. Write a symmetric object-layer pair matrix and test both `(A, B)` and `(B, A)`. Separately map object layers to broad-phase layers and implement object-vs-broad-phase pruning. Add query and sensor-mask tests; they are not implied by the collision-pair matrix.

Where a query, callback, collector, or active-body list can be unordered, convert its results to stable host identities and sort or otherwise canonically normalize them before gameplay, rollback, or hashing observes the sequence.

### 4. Wrap bodies with stable host identity and safe access

Give each gameplay object a stable host ID plus generation, and maintain a mapping to the current world-local `BodyID`. Invalidate that mapping on removal/destruction. Apply spawns, despawns, and other structural mutations only at owned fixed-tick boundaries and retain them as ordered events.

Implement the complete `CreateBody` -> `AddBody` -> `RemoveBody` -> `DestroyBody` lifecycle. Every lock can fail for a stale or destroyed ID, so check lock success before dereferencing. Use `BodyLockMultiRead`/`BodyLockMultiWrite` for multi-body operations. Permit no-lock access only through a wrapper whose documented callback or already-held-lock precondition proves it safe.

### 5. Give simulation one fixed-step owner

The render loop contributes elapsed time to one accumulator. Consume fixed ticks with `deltaTime = 1 / 120`, calling:

```cpp
physics_system.Update(1.0f / 120.0f, collision_steps,
                      temp_allocator, job_system);
```

Measure `collision_steps` on representative content. Bound catch-up ticks and define an overload policy that does not stretch the simulation delta; presentation should interpolate independently. Read the returned `EPhysicsUpdateError` flags on every tick. For allocator, contact, or body-pair capacity failures, define whether the engine stops, degrades, resizes at a safe boundary, or requests resynchronization. Record capacity and memory high-water marks instead of adopting HelloWorld's counts or 10 MiB temporary allocator as production defaults.

### 6. Build rollback around host structure, not raw handles

At each rollback frame retain:

- the Jolt `StateRecorder` stream;
- stable-host-ID/generation to current-`BodyID` mapping;
- ordered structural create/add/remove/destroy events;
- tick-stamped inputs and their total order;
- character, vehicle, and other gameplay state outside the recorder;
- content/config/build compatibility metadata; and
- update-error and recovery metadata.

To restore, first recreate the matching structure and IDs in the recorded call order, then restore the compatible Jolt state, then replay the normalized ordered inputs/events. Never transmit raw `BodyID` as authoritative identity. Hash diagnostic state at tick boundaries and retain an authoritative correction/resync path when reconstruction or replay diverges.

### 7. Integrate each optional module at its actual seam

For `CharacterVirtual`, keep the object host-owned and drive its v5.6 `Update`/`ExtendedUpdate` path once per fixed tick. Install and retain a `CharacterContactListener`, and snapshot controller inputs, listener-derived/contact state, supporting-body state, and any external movement state needed by rollback. Because a virtual character is not a rigid body, decide explicitly how ordinary queries and rigid bodies see the player. If an optional inner body is used, document which visibility and contacts it represents and test that mapping.

For each `VehicleConstraint`, retain its chassis, controller, `VehicleCollisionTester`, and relevant listeners. Register it with both `AddConstraint` and `AddStepListener`, and apply inputs at a fixed declared point in the tick. Teardown must call `RemoveStepListener` and `RemoveConstraint` before destroying the vehicle, collision tester, controller, or chassis. Store external vehicle input/state for rollback, never a raw constraint pointer.

For cloth, retain immutable/shared `SoftBodySharedSettings`, create per-instance `SoftBodyCreationSettings`, and create through `CreateAndAddSoftBody`. Check `IsSoftBody` before type-specific access, use `SoftBodyMotionProperties`, and route contacts through `SoftBodyContactListener`. Do not assume ordinary constraints or all regular-body APIs apply: v5.6 soft bodies are WIP, have no simulated soft-soft response, and require explicit CPU, memory, collision, recovery, and networking-scope validation. Decide whether cloth is local-only, server-authoritative, or replicated before treating it as rollback state.

### 8. Prove determinism rather than declaring it

Enable `JPH_CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC` in every compatible target build and make source, defines, precision, SIMD/FP policy, content, inputs, and command order identical. Stabilize all host command submission and normalize query, collector, callback/contact, and active-body result order before it affects simulation-facing gameplay.

Build an evidence matrix across every supported Windows/Linux compiler, architecture, and build role. Establish same-binary repeatability first, then replay the same tick-stamped inputs and ordered structural events on each target. Capture a per-tick state hash and the first divergent tick, together with inputs, structural events, job configuration, `EPhysicsUpdateError` flags, and normalized result sets. Use those artifacts to bisect divergence. A matching seed is only one input to this test.

## Validation and ship gates

Promote the integration through these gates in order:

1. Build and run pinned v5.6.0 HelloWorld as an initialization/update/shutdown smoke test.
2. Run upstream UnitTests for every supported compiler, define set, precision mode, architecture, and build role.
3. Run official Samples covering every used API: layer/filter/query behavior, bodies and constraints, `CharacterVirtual`, vehicles, and soft bodies.
4. Run pinned determinism and `StateRecorder` save/restore tests. Inject mismatched structure, stale IDs, capacity errors, and allocator/job faults and verify the declared recovery paths.
5. Run host tests for the 120 Hz accumulator, interpolation separation, bounded backlog, spawn/despawn rollback, per-tick hashes, deliberate divergence, authority/resync, callback threading, repeated shutdown, and replay under jitter, packet loss, and reordering.
6. Run `PerformanceTest` and the host profiler on target builds with target content. Report p50/p95/p99 physics tick time, worst catch-up behavior, and measured budgets/high-water marks for temporary memory, jobs/barriers, bodies, pairs, contacts, constraints, rollback memory, and bandwidth.

Shipping requires every used module and every supported platform/build role to pass its relevant gates, with no ignored update-error flags and with deterministic or authoritative-recovery behavior demonstrated. HelloWorld remains the first rung, not the release criterion.

Jolt does not invent an engine thread budget or own the integration's worker policy: the host must create and retain the temporary allocator and `JobSystem`, choose their capacities/thread count, define callback-thread rules and barriers, and handle allocator/job failures. 2. **One broad object layer with all pairs enabled is not a real collision design.** `ObjectLayer` is the gameplay pair policy, `BroadPhaseLayer` is a storage partition, `ObjectVsBroadPhaseLayerFilter` prunes object-layer queries against those partitions, and `ObjectLayerPairFilter` makes object-pair collision decisions. These are distinct seams. An everything-collides configuration is likely both semantically wrong and unnecessarily expensive.

3. **`BodyID` cannot be permanent identity.** It is local to one `PhysicsSystem`, includes reuse protection, and can eventually be reused. The required lifetime is `CreateBody -> AddBody -> RemoveBody -> DestroyBody`. A stale ID can make a lock fail, so the result must be checked before dereferencing. Raw `BodyID` values must not be used as network IDs or durable save identities.

4. **The variable render-loop update is incompatible with a 120 Hz simulation contract.** One host scheduler must own a fixed-step accumulator and call Jolt once per consumed physics tick with `deltaTime = 1 / 120`. Presentation interpolation is separate. Catch-up must be bounded, with an explicit backlog/overload policy that does not stretch the simulation delta. In v5.6 the second argument is `collisionSteps`; it is not a spare integration-substep parameter.

5. **Raw IDs plus transforms are not rollback state.** Jolt `SaveState`/`RestoreState` through `StateRecorder` cover simulation state but not host configuration, gameplay state, or bodies added/removed between snapshots. Restore requires matching structure, compatible settings, matching IDs, and matching call order. Transform-only snapshots omit velocities, sleep/contact/constraint state, module state, and structural history.

6. **A common random seed does not establish Windows/Linux determinism.** `JPH_CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC` is a prerequisite, not a guarantee. Source, defines, precision, SIMD/FP behavior, content, tick-stamped inputs, structural call order, and any thread-visible ordering must also agree. Broad-phase queries, collectors, callbacks/contacts, and active-body results must be normalized before gameplay or hashes consume them.

7. **The optional modules need explicit integration contracts.** `CharacterVirtual` is not an ordinary rigid body; normal rigid-body queries and bodies do not automatically see it. A vehicle must be registered as both a constraint and a step listener. Soft bodies have type-specific creation, lifetime, motion, and contact APIs and remain WIP in v5.6. Merely constructing these objects is insufficient.

## Corrected integration plan

### 1. Freeze and reproduce the build

Create a build manifest for every client/server target containing:

- exact Jolt tag and commit;
- compiler, standard library, platform, architecture, and build role;
- float/double precision, SIMD and floating-point policy;
- all Jolt and host defines, including whether `JPH_CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC` is enabled;
- allocator implementation, job implementation and worker count;
- enabled modules, content/config revision, and capture provenance.

Verify compatible definitions across every translation unit. Treat binary saved state as pinned-version data, not a cross-version storage format. In particular, do not mix older update/substep guidance with the v5.6 API, and regression-test the v5.6 friction and callback/API boundaries.

### 2. Establish process, world, and shutdown ownership

Initialize in dependency order:

1. Call `JPH::RegisterDefaultAllocator` before any other Jolt use, and install host trace/assert hooks.
2. Set `JPH::Factory::sInstance = new JPH::Factory`, then call `JPH::RegisterTypes()`.
3. Create long-lived host-owned temporary allocator, `JobSystem`, broad-phase interface, object-vs-broad-phase filter, object-pair filter, and listeners.
4. Construct the `PhysicsSystem`, call `Init` with measured capacities and the retained filters, attach listeners, and only then create/add bodies and constraints.

The engine chooses the worker count and owns submission/barrier policy. Document which callbacks may execute on workers, which host services are callback-safe, and what happens on temporary-memory exhaustion, queue/barrier failure, or shutdown.

Shutdown must first stop tick submission and callbacks, join workers, remove/destroy constraints and bodies, unregister listeners, destroy worlds and their retained dependencies, call `JPH::UnregisterTypes()`, then delete and clear `Factory::sInstance`. Repeated initialize/world-create/world-destroy/shutdown tests should detect dangling callbacks and lifetime inversions.

### 3. Define collision layers from gameplay requirements

Write a symmetric source-controlled `ObjectLayer` pair matrix—for example, static world, dynamic bodies, players, vehicles, sensors, and any projectile/query categories actually needed. Deliberately map those object layers into broad-phase layers. Implement the `ObjectVsBroadPhaseLayerFilter` and `ObjectLayerPairFilter` separately.

Test every allowed and rejected object-pair combination in both argument orders, plus query and sensor masks. Treat collected query results as unordered sets; before deterministic gameplay, rollback logging, or hashing, map results to stable host IDs and sort by that identity.

### 4. Put body structure behind a fixed-tick command boundary

Give every replicated entity a stable host ID plus generation and maintain a mapping to its current `BodyID`. Perform spawn/add/remove/destroy only in a deterministic, total-ordered command stream at owned tick boundaries. Invalidate the mapping when a body is removed/destroyed and never retain a raw Jolt handle as durable identity.

Use locking accessors that report failure for stale IDs. For multi-body operations use `BodyLockMultiRead` or `BodyLockMultiWrite` so lock acquisition order is controlled. Expose no-lock access only through a wrapper whose precondition proves that the caller already has the required lock or callback guarantee.

### 5. Run one authoritative 120 Hz scheduler

Accumulate elapsed real time in the host, consume fixed ticks of exactly `1 / 120`, and leave render interpolation outside physics. Put input sampling, structural commands, controller/vehicle input, Jolt update, event collection/normalization, snapshotting, and hashing in one documented per-tick order. Bound the number of catch-up ticks and declare whether overload causes a pause, drop/resync, or other explicit recovery; do not enlarge the fixed delta.

For v5.6, a tick should resemble:

```cpp
constexpr float fixed_delta = 1.0f / 120.0f;
JPH::EPhysicsUpdateError errors = physics_system.Update(
    fixed_delta, collision_steps, &temp_allocator, &job_system);
```

Choose `collision_steps` from testing rather than copying a sample. Inspect every returned `EPhysicsUpdateError` flag on every tick. Define a safe policy for allocator, contact, or body-pair capacity failures—stop, controlled degradation, resizing at a safe boundary, or authoritative resync. Silently continuing makes rollback/determinism results untrustworthy. Size capacities and the temporary allocator from observed high-water marks; HelloWorld's values and 10 MiB allocator are examples only.

### 6. Design rollback around structure as well as state

At each rollback frame retain:

- the Jolt `StateRecorder` stream;
- stable-host-ID/generation to `BodyID` mapping;
- the total-ordered spawn/add/remove/destroy event stream;
- tick-stamped inputs;
- host gameplay, `CharacterVirtual`, vehicle, and other state outside the recorder;
- content/config/build version and recovery metadata;
- update error flags and a diagnostic state hash.

To restore, first reproduce the recorded world structure and IDs in the recorded call order, then restore the compatible Jolt state, restore host/module state, and replay the same ordered commands. Test stale IDs and mismatched structure explicitly. If restore or replay diverges, retain the first divergent tick and fall back to authoritative correction/resync rather than continuing silently.

### 7. Integrate each optional module at its real seam

- **Players / `CharacterVirtual`:** keep it host-owned and drive `Update` or `ExtendedUpdate` explicitly once per fixed tick. Install the v5.6 `CharacterContactListener`. Retain inputs, supporting-body state, listener payloads, and all external controller state for rollback. Decide whether gameplay requires the optional inner body; document which queries/contacts see the virtual character and which see the inner body.
- **Cars / `VehicleConstraint`:** retain the chassis, vehicle, controller, `VehicleCollisionTester`, and listeners. Register with both `AddConstraint` and `AddStepListener`, apply controller inputs at a fixed point in the tick, and retain external input/state for rollback. Teardown calls `RemoveStepListener` and `RemoveConstraint` before destroying the vehicle, tester, controller, or chassis.
- **Cloth / soft bodies:** keep immutable/shared `SoftBodySharedSettings` alive, combine them with per-instance `SoftBodyCreationSettings`, and create using `CreateAndAddSoftBody`. Check `IsSoftBody` before type-specific access, use `SoftBodyMotionProperties`, and route contacts through `SoftBodyContactListener`. Do not assume regular rigid-body or constraint behavior applies. In v5.6 there is no simulated soft-soft response and the feature is WIP, so explicitly choose local-only, authoritative, or replicated scope and gate shipment on CPU, memory, collision, rollback/recovery, and networking evidence.

### 8. Prove determinism instead of assuming it

First establish same-binary deterministic replay. Then run identical tick-stamped inputs and structural commands across every supported Windows/Linux compiler, architecture, and build role using the frozen manifest. Keep command order stable, normalize unordered result sources, and record per-tick hashes. On divergence, preserve the first bad tick, inputs, structural events, job configuration, update error flags, and normalized query/callback/active-body sets so the mismatch is reproducible and bisectable.

## Validation and release gates

Run the following ladder in order, promoting a target only when every used module and supported build role passes:

1. Build and run pinned v5.6.0 HelloWorld for initialization, update, and shutdown smoke coverage.
2. Run upstream UnitTests with the exact selected compiler, defines, precision, and FP/SIMD policy.
3. Run official Samples covering the actual APIs used: layers/queries, rigid bodies/constraints, `CharacterVirtual`, vehicles, and soft bodies.
4. Run determinism and `StateRecorder` save/restore tests, including mismatched structure, stale/reused IDs, capacity errors, and allocator/job fault injection.
5. Run host tests for fixed stepping, bounded backlog, spawn/despawn ordering, rollback/replay, hash divergence, callback threading, repeated shutdown, and authority/resync under jitter, loss, and reordering.
6. Run PerformanceTest and the host profiler on target hardware, builds, and representative content. Report p50/p95/p99 physics tick time and budgets/high-water marks for temporary memory, jobs/barriers, bodies, pairs, constraints, contacts, rollback memory, and network bandwidth.

Shipment should require this evidence matrix, explicit policies for every `EPhysicsUpdateError`, and passing module-specific tests. A seed and a passing HelloWorld run are not release criteria.

```cpp
constexpr float fixed_delta = 1.0f / 120.0f;

while (accumulator >= fixed_delta && ticks_this_frame < max_catch_up_ticks)
{
    ApplyTickStampedInputsAndStructuralEvents(next_tick);
    UpdateCharactersVehiclesAndGameplayInDeclaredOrder(fixed_delta);
```

- stable host identity mappings and active/removed state;
- ordered spawn/add/remove/destroy and other structural events;

- content/config/build version and recovery metadata; and

In deterministic paths use Jolt Sin/Cos, `QuickSort`, `BinaryHeapPush`/`BinaryHeapPop`, and `Hash` instead of the corresponding standard-library operations.

## Review of the current plan

| Current assumption | Required correction |
|---|---|
| Allocator and `Factory` are sufficient initialization | Call `RegisterDefaultAllocator` before any Jolt API, install diagnostics, create `Factory`, call `RegisterTypes`, construct all long-lived dependencies, then initialize the world. Reverse this dependency order during shutdown. |
| Jolt creates its own worker threads | The application owns and supplies the `JobSystem`, its thread budget, barriers, shutdown behavior, and callback-thread contract. |
| One object layer with all pairs colliding | Separate gameplay collision policy from broad-phase partitioning. Implement a symmetric `ObjectLayerPairFilter`, deliberate object-to-broad-phase mapping, and an `ObjectVsBroadPhaseLayerFilter`. Test sensors and query masks separately. |
| `BodyID` can be retained forever | `BodyID` is world-local and reusable after destruction. Keep a stable engine/network entity ID and a validated host mapping. `RemoveBody` preserves the ID; `DestroyBody` invalidates it. |
| Raw `BodyID` plus transforms is a rollback snapshot | Transforms omit velocities, sleep state, contacts, cached simulation state, structural history, and host-owned controller state. Use `StateRecorder` plus host state and ordered structural events. Never use raw `BodyID` as network identity. |
| Call `Update` from a variable render loop | Run a single fixed-step accumulator at exactly `1 / 120` seconds. Render with interpolation. Bound catch-up work without stretching the simulation delta. |
| Same seed implies Windows/Linux determinism | A seed is only one input. Determinism also requires a pinned source/build, matching defines and call order, controlled floating-point behavior, deterministic host utilities, normalized queries/events, and cross-platform evidence. |
| HelloWorld passing is sufficient | HelloWorld is only an initialization smoke test. Shipping requires upstream tests, used samples, rollback/determinism/fault tests, network tests, and target performance evidence. |

## 1. Freeze the actual integration target

Pin the integration to a verified release, not `master`. The current source contract should be recorded as Jolt v5.6.0, commit `e77f175595e64cb44218cc9d9d56fc365ad0e36a`, but verify that this is actually what the executable contains.

- Jolt tag and commit
- compiler, standard library, platform, and architecture
- float or double precision
- SIMD and floating-point policies
- every Jolt and host compile definition
- debug/profile/release role
- allocator and job-system implementations
- worker count and job scheduling configuration
- enabled modules
- content/configuration revision
- provenance of the binary used for a test capture

Verify that every translation unit sees compatible Jolt definitions. Do not assume older signatures or substep recommendations apply: v5.6 `PhysicsSystem::Update` takes `collisionSteps`, followed by `TempAllocator*` and `JobSystem*`. Friction and several module APIs also changed at this boundary.

## 2. Correct process and world lifecycle

Initialization should follow dependency order:

1. Call `JPH::RegisterDefaultAllocator()` before any Jolt allocation or API use.
2. Install the host trace and assertion hooks.
3. Create `JPH::Factory::sInstance`.
4. Call `JPH::RegisterTypes()`.
5. Construct the long-lived temporary allocator and application-owned `JobSystem`.
6. Construct and retain the broad-phase interface, pair filter, object-vs-broad-phase filter, and listeners.
7. Construct the `PhysicsSystem` and call `Init` with measured capacities.
8. Register listeners.
9. Create and add bodies, constraints, characters, and vehicles.

If `JobSystemThreadPool` is used, configure its thread count explicitly from an engine budget. Document which callbacks can execute on worker threads, how jobs are drained, and what happens on job or allocator failure.

Shutdown must stop new updates and callbacks first, drain/join workers, unregister step listeners and constraints, remove/destroy bodies, unregister remaining listeners, destroy the world and retained dependencies, then:

```cpp
JPH::UnregisterTypes();
delete JPH::Factory::sInstance;
JPH::Factory::sInstance = nullptr;
```

Add repeated initialize/run/shutdown tests to expose dangling callbacks and incorrect ownership.

## 3. Define layers and filters deliberately

Create a source-controlled object-layer collision matrix for categories such as static geometry, dynamic bodies, sensors, character proxies, vehicles, and soft bodies. The exact categories are game-specific, but the policy must be symmetric:

```text
collides(A, B) == collides(B, A)
```

Then independently define:

- `ObjectLayerPairFilter`: whether two object layers may collide.
- `BroadPhaseLayerInterface`: where each object layer is stored.
- `ObjectVsBroadPhaseLayerFilter`: which broad-phase partitions an object/query must inspect.
- Query and sensor masks: what gameplay queries and triggers are allowed to observe.

Test every matrix entry in both argument orders. One all-colliding layer hides mistakes and prevents useful broad-phase pruning.

For deterministic broad-phase result processing, sorting returned IDs is insufficient because widened broad-phase bounds can change hit membership. Use a custom `CollisionCollector::AddHit` that re-tests the original query against `Body::GetWorldSpaceBounds`, rejects false broad-phase candidates, and then orders accepted results by stable engine identity. Normalize narrow-phase results, callback events, and active-body results too.

## 4. Introduce safe host body handles

Use a host handle similar to:

```text
PhysicsEntityHandle {
    stable engine/network entity ID
    world ID
    host generation
    current BodyID
    active/removed/destroyed state
}
```

The lifecycle is:

```text
CreateBody -> AddBody -> RemoveBody -> optional AddBody -> DestroyBody
```

For objects that may reappear during the rollback window, prefer removing them and defer final destruction until they fall outside that window. Network messages should use stable entity ID plus generation, never serialized raw `BodyID`.

Maintain the accumulator in high precision and simulate only fixed ticks:

```cpp
constexpr float kFixedDelta = 1.0f / 120.0f;

accumulator += render_frame_seconds;
uint32_t catch_up_steps = 0;

while (accumulator >= kFixedDelta &&
       catch_up_steps < max_catch_up_steps)
{
    ApplyTickStampedCommandsInStableOrder(tick);
    ApplyStructuralEventsInStableOrder(tick);
    UpdateHostOwnedControllersForTick(tick);

    JPH::EPhysicsUpdateError errors = physics_system.Update(
        kFixedDelta,
        collision_steps,
        &temp_allocator,
        &job_system);

    HandleUpdateErrors(errors);
    CommitNormalizedPhysicsEvents(tick);
    CaptureRollbackStateAndHash(tick);

    accumulator -= kFixedDelta;
    ++tick;
    ++catch_up_steps;
}

render_alpha = accumulator / kFixedDelta;
```

If the backlog exceeds the catch-up budget, invoke an explicit overload policy—such as pausing presentation, requesting authoritative resynchronization, or terminating an unhealthy session. Do not enlarge the fixed delta to catch up.

Inspect every `EPhysicsUpdateError` bit on every tick:
